Editorial/source appendices glued onto the Japanese hee1 text (e.g. '(IMP-24 で追加…)', '(Added in S-004. Sources: …)', trailing URLs and Wikipedia-editor credits, stray '）', 'CHEMISTRY #142', '（枝 [B-xx] 候補）', '（[7-08] から移動）') were not translated as child-facing text; affected keys include 0-18, 1-48..1-76, 2-24, 2-45..2-56, 2-62..2-64, 3-14, 3-21..3-24, 4-15..4-33, 4-37, 7-22..7-28, 8-19..8-42, 9-41..9-49, 10-17..10-39, 11-17, 12-16..12-18, 13-16, 14-15..14-21, 15-16..15-33, B-05, B-18..B-23. Source oddities to check: 1-26.hee1 and 6-02.hee1 pack all four hee levels into one string; I-54.name looks truncated ('…回路図で考え'); P-37 (city bus) hee1 is the turbocharger text. Spelling: American English throughout (aluminum, color), so 1-29.name is 'Aluminum'.

strings.0-01.name: Knapped stone tools
strings.0-01.hee1: Hit a stone with another stone and it breaks, leaving an edge as sharp as a knife. The surest proof is 2.6 million years old (some say 3.3 million ⚠️).
strings.0-02.name: Fire making
strings.0-02.hee1: Rub two pieces of wood together and they get hot, and at last a fire starts.
strings.0-03.name: Earthenware
strings.0-03.hee1: Once clay is fired, water can never turn it back. People knew this 20,000 years ago.
strings.0-04.name: Farming
strings.0-04.hee1: Fields began when people kept picking and growing the wheat whose grains did not fall off easily.
strings.0-05.name: Beans
strings.0-05.hee1: Bean roots have tiny germs that turn nitrogen from the air into fertilizer, so the field does not wear out easily.
strings.0-06.name: Weaving
strings.0-06.hee1: Soak flax stems in water until they rot, and you get fibers for making thread for cloth.
strings.0-07.name: Wool and the spindle whorl
strings.0-07.hee1: A little "flywheel" that spins like a top was used to twist wool into thread.
strings.0-08.name: Woodworking
strings.0-08.hee1: Grind a stone axe and you get an edge that does not chip so easily.
strings.0-09.name: Wheel
strings.0-09.hee1: Before the wheel, there was the potter's wheel, a turning table for making pottery.
strings.0-10.name: Lime burning
strings.0-10.hee1: You can make it by burning seashells. It is what wall plaster is made from.
strings.0-11.name: Slaked lime and lime plaster
strings.0-11.hee1: Slaked lime soaks up carbon dioxide from the air, turns back into stone, and sets hard.
strings.0-12.name: Charcoal
strings.0-12.hee1: Burn wood where there is little air, and what is left is charcoal, which is mostly carbon.
strings.0-13.name: Cart
strings.0-13.hee1: A four-wheeled cart pulled by oxen. People rubbed animal fat on the axles to make them turn smoothly.
strings.0-14.name: Water transport
strings.0-14.hee1: Heavy stones and ores are much easier to float along on water than to carry over land.
strings.0-15.name: Kiln
strings.0-15.hee1: Surround a fire with walls and it gets hotter than an open fire. That heat made it possible to melt copper.
strings.0-16.name: Salt pans
strings.0-16.hee1: From nigari, the bitter liquid used to set tofu, you can get magnesium, the metal used in airplanes.
strings.0-17.name: Domestication
strings.0-17.hee1: The ancestor of cattle was the wild aurochs, nearly 2 m tall at the shoulder.
strings.0-18.name: Rope
strings.0-18.hee1: Even thin fibers can hold up heavy things once you twist them together.
strings.0-19.name: Potter's wheel
strings.0-19.hee1: Before the cart wheel, there was a spinning table for making pottery: the potter's wheel.
strings.1-01.name: Germanium from coal ash
strings.1-01.hee1: The ash left after burning coal sometimes has germanium gathered in it.
strings.1-02.name: Native copper
strings.1-02.hee1: Some copper was found in the ground already as metal. Hammering makes it hard; heating makes it soft again.
strings.1-03.name: Copper smelting (malachite)
strings.1-03.hee1: Heat a green stone (malachite) with charcoal, and copper comes out.
strings.1-04.name: Copper smelting (chalcopyrite)
strings.1-04.hee1: Most copper today comes from ores joined with sulfur, by blowing air through them.
strings.1-05.name: Bronze
strings.1-05.hee1: Mix 10% tin into copper and you get bronze, which melts easily yet is hard.
strings.1-06.name: Bloomery
strings.1-06.hee1: Old furnaces could not melt iron, so it came out as a spongy lump.
strings.1-07.name: Graphite
strings.1-07.hee1: Graphite, the same stuff as pencil lead, was also used to make crucibles that stand up to heat.
strings.1-08.name: Wrought iron
strings.1-08.hee1: Hammer red-hot iron, and the dirt mixed inside gets squeezed out.
strings.1-09.name: Blast furnace (pig iron)
strings.1-09.hee1: Make the furnace taller and blow in more air, and the iron melts and flows out.
strings.1-10.name: Coke blast furnace
strings.1-10.hee1: When the forests ran short of wood, people started making iron with coke, which is coal baked without air.
strings.1-11.name: Crucible steel
strings.1-11.hee1: Melt iron completely in a covered crucible and you get smooth, even steel. It was used for clock springs.
strings.1-12.name: Open-hearth furnace
strings.1-12.hee1: A furnace that can melt scrap iron too, and slowly adjust what is in the steel.
strings.1-13.name: Zinc
strings.1-13.hee1: In an ordinary furnace zinc turns into gas and escapes, so people cooled it down to collect it.
strings.1-14.name: Bayer process
strings.1-14.hee1: Bauxite is dissolved in sodium hydroxide, the red iron-rich mud is filtered out, and alumina is taken out.
strings.1-15.name: Metallurgical silicon
strings.1-15.hee1: Silicon is made from "stone", "charcoal" and "lots of electricity".
strings.1-16.name: Trichlorosilane synthesis and distillation
strings.1-16.hee1: Silicon is first turned into a liquid that boils at 32°C, then cleaned by distillation.
strings.1-17.name: Siemens process
strings.1-17.hee1: A thin, hot silicon rod keeps growing thicker inside the gas.
strings.1-18.name: Platinum refining
strings.1-18.hee1: By pressing platinum powder together and hammering it, people got a metal they could work with.
strings.1-19.name: Rare earth separation
strings.1-19.hee1: Rare earths are so alike that they are separated by using tiny differences, repeated hundreds of times.
strings.1-20.name: Platinum
strings.1-20.hee1: Platinum is found as tiny bits of metal mixed in river sand.
strings.1-21.name: Fluorite CaF2
strings.1-21.hee1: Fluorite is found in ore veins together with galena and sphalerite.
strings.1-22.name: Cassiterite SnO2
strings.1-22.hee1: Tin ore is found near granite and in river sand.
strings.1-23.name: Molybdenite MoS2
strings.1-23.hee1: Molybdenum ore comes out as a side product of copper mines.
strings.1-24.name: Bauxite
strings.1-24.hee1: Bauxite, the raw material for aluminum, is soil made when rocks weather away in hot countries.
strings.1-25.name: Monazite
strings.1-25.hee1: Monazite is collected from sand together with iron sand.
strings.1-26.name: Steel
strings.1-26.hee1: 1) Just blowing air into iron turns it into steel. The color of the flame tells you when it is done. 2) Pig iron 4% → steel 0.1–0.5%, with no fuel. 3) Bessemer 1856 and Kelly; steel became cheap, and rails and bridges became steel. 4) Mushet's spiegeleisen; the phosphorus problem → Thomas 1878.
strings.1-27.name: Lead
strings.1-27.hee1: The metal of old water pipes and printing type. It is bad for your body.
strings.1-28.name: Tungsten wire
strings.1-28.hee1: Its melting point is 3400°C, too hot to melt, so the powder is pressed and baked solid.
strings.1-29.name: Aluminum
strings.1-29.hee1: Until then aluminum cost more than gold, and Napoleon III used it as tableware for honored guests.
strings.1-30.name: Tin
strings.1-30.hee1: A material for bronze 5,000 years ago becomes the light source for cutting-edge EUV.
strings.1-31.name: Molybdenum smelting
strings.1-31.hee1: The SO2 given off by roasting can be sent on to make sulfuric acid [2-01].
strings.1-32.name: Silver
strings.1-32.hee1: The Iwami Silver Mine also got its silver out by cupellation.
strings.1-33.name: Boron
strings.1-33.hee1: Borax has long been used as a "flux" for brazing metals.
strings.1-34.name: Germanium tetrachloride distillation
strings.1-34.hee1: Germanium is turned into a liquid that boils at 83°C, then cleaned by distillation.
strings.1-35.name: Neodymium magnet
strings.1-35.hee1: A magnet made of neodymium, iron and boron. It was born in Japan and the USA at almost the same time.
strings.1-36.name: Elemental boron
strings.1-36.hee1: Magnesium is made to steal the oxygen, and boron is left behind.
strings.1-37.name: Nickel
strings.1-37.hee1: Nickel turns into a gas with carbon monoxide, and when heated it turns back into pure nickel.
strings.1-38.name: Synthetic cryolite
strings.1-38.hee1: Natural cryolite was only found in Greenland, so now it is made by chemistry.
strings.1-39.name: Magnesium
strings.1-39.hee1: 1 L of seawater holds about 1.3 g of Mg. The Mg for aircraft in World War II was taken from the sea.
strings.1-40.name: Chromium
strings.1-40.hee1: Thermite is still used today to weld railway rails on the spot.
strings.1-41.name: Titanium
strings.1-41.hee1: From the black grains mixed into iron sand comes the metal used for airplane frames.
strings.1-42.name: Lithium
strings.1-42.hee1: Lithium is a metal so light that it floats on water.
strings.1-43.name: Antimony
strings.1-43.hee1: Like water, antimony swells a little when it sets solid (so the edges of printing type come out sharp).
strings.1-44.name: Gallium
strings.1-44.hee1: Gallium melts from the warmth of your palm (melting point about 30°C).
strings.1-45.name: Mercury
strings.1-45.hee1: What is inside a thermometer. Do not touch it.
strings.1-46.name: Quartzite
strings.1-46.hee1: A vein where white quartz filled a crack in the rock.
strings.1-47.name: Lodestone
strings.1-47.hee1: The first magnets were stones dug out of the ground.
strings.1-48.name: Basic oxygen furnace
strings.1-48.hee1: Blow in oxygen instead of air, and steel is made in a few tens of minutes.
strings.1-49.name: Electric arc steelmaking
strings.1-49.hee1: Old scrap iron is melted with electric sparks and made into new steel.
strings.1-50.name: Continuous casting
strings.1-50.hee1: The steel keeps flowing without stopping, and a long slab is pulled out of the mold.
strings.1-51.name: Rolling
strings.1-51.hee1: Pass iron between two turning rollers and it quickly gets thinner and longer.
strings.1-52.name: Extrusion
strings.1-52.hee1: Push it out like noodles through a press, and you get long aluminum bars all the same shape.
strings.1-53.name: Ferrite
strings.1-53.hee1: The black magnets on your fridge are ferrite magnets, made like pottery.
strings.1-54.name: Invar
strings.1-54.hee1: Just by mixing nickel into iron, you get a metal whose length hardly changes in summer or winter.
strings.1-55.name: Synthetic diamond
strings.1-55.hee1: Most diamonds used in factories are synthetic diamonds made by squeezing graphite very hard.
strings.1-56.name: Steam hammer
strings.1-56.hee1: Huge lumps of steel that no human arm could strike can be hit with 100 tons of force by a hammer driven by steam.
strings.1-57.name: Carbon fiber
strings.1-57.hee1: Carbon fiber weighs about a quarter as much as iron, yet is stronger than iron ⚠️
strings.1-58.name: Wire drawing
strings.1-58.hee1: The copper wire in electric cables is made by pulling a thick rod through small holes dozens of times until it is thin.
strings.1-59.name: Puddling process
strings.1-59.hee1: The iron of the Eiffel Tower is wrought iron, made by workers stirring the iron inside a furnace with a rod.
strings.1-60.name: Electrolytic copper refining
strings.1-60.hee1: The copper in electric wires is made 99.99% pure by electrolysis.
strings.1-61.name: Thomas process
strings.1-61.hee1: The phosphorus slag taken out of the iron became fertilizer for fields.
strings.1-62.name: Stainless steel
strings.1-62.hee1: Stainless steel does not rust because an invisibly thin film of chromium forms on its surface and protects it.
strings.1-63.name: Manganese addition
strings.1-63.hee1: Adding just a little manganese made steel that used to crack easily strong.
strings.1-64.name: Gold extraction
strings.1-64.hee1: One ton of gold ore often holds only a few grams of gold ⚠️
strings.1-65.name: High-speed steel
strings.1-65.hee1: A high-speed steel blade stays sharp even when it gets hot enough to glow red.
strings.1-66.name: Tantalum
strings.1-66.hee1: Light bulb filaments changed from carbon to tantalum to tungsten, each one standing up to heat better.
strings.1-67.name: Froth flotation
strings.1-67.hee1: The grains of metal in ore stick to bubbles and float up.
strings.1-68.name: Permanent magnet steel
strings.1-68.hee1: A magnet steel made by Japanese researchers was the strongest magnet in the world at the time.
strings.1-69.name: Carburizing and nitriding
strings.1-69.hee1: Only the surface of a gear is made hard, while the inside stays tough and hard to crack.
strings.1-70.name: Zirconium and hafnium
strings.1-70.hee1: Hafnium was found only after a way of studying elements with X-rays was invented.
strings.1-71.name: Heat treatment
strings.1-71.hee1: The same steel can end up with completely different hardness just by changing how fast you cool it.
strings.1-72.name: Powder metallurgy and hot isostatic pressing
strings.1-72.hee1: Metals that are very hard to melt are shaped by pressing their powder and baking it.
strings.1-73.name: Coated steel sheet
strings.1-73.hee1: The zinc on galvanized sheet rusts first itself, protecting the iron underneath.
strings.1-74.name: Cemented carbide
strings.1-74.hee1: The cemented carbide name "Widia" means "like diamond" in German.
strings.1-75.name: Vacuum degassing
strings.1-75.hee1: Suck molten steel up into a vacuum, and the gas hiding inside comes out as bubbles.
strings.1-76.name: Direct reduced iron
strings.1-76.hee1: Make iron with hydrogen, and what comes out of the chimney is water, not carbon dioxide.
strings.2-01.name: Sulfuric acid
strings.2-01.hee1: Join oxygen to sulfur dioxide and let water soak it up, and you get sulfuric acid.
strings.2-02.name: Potash
strings.2-02.hee1: The name potassium comes from "pot ash", the ash left in a pot.
strings.2-03.name: Natural soda
strings.2-03.hee1: A salt that was even used for making mummies in ancient Egypt.
strings.2-04.name: Kelp ash soda
strings.2-04.hee1: Soda was taken from seaweed ash, and iodine was found in the liquid from that ash too.
strings.2-05.name: Leblanc process
strings.2-05.hee1: A way to make soda from salt and sulfuric acid. The hydrochloric acid gas it gave off was at first just let out into the sky.
strings.2-06.name: Solvay process
strings.2-06.hee1: Soda is made from salt, ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia is collected and used again.
strings.2-07.name: Potassium dichromate
strings.2-07.hee1: The name chromium comes from the Greek word for "color", because it makes compounds of many colors.
strings.2-08.name: Caustic soda
strings.2-08.hee1: Mix soda with slaked lime and you get caustic soda.
strings.2-09.name: Soap
strings.2-09.hee1: Mix oil with a strong alkali and you get soap.
strings.2-10.name: Hydrofluoric acid
strings.2-10.hee1: Hydrofluoric acid dissolves glass, so it cannot be kept in a glass bottle.
strings.2-11.name: Hydrogen sulfide and sulfur recovery
strings.2-11.hee1: Sulfur was won back from the waste of soda factories.
strings.2-12.name: Sulfates
strings.2-12.hee1: Pass electricity through copper sulfate solution, and copper sticks onto a mold in its shape.
strings.2-13.name: Lime cycle and calcium chloride
strings.2-13.hee1: Lime is burned, splashed with water, and turns back into stone in the air. It can be used round and round.
strings.2-14.name: Soda-lime glass
strings.2-14.hee1: Sand alone needs 1700°C, but mix in soda and it melts at 1000°C.
strings.2-15.name: Borosilicate glass
strings.2-15.hee1: The beakers in a science room do not crack over a flame, thanks to boron.
strings.2-16.name: Distilled water
strings.2-16.hee1: Boil water and cool the steam, and you get water with no salt left in it.
strings.2-17.name: Ion exchange
strings.2-17.hee1: A relative of Bakelite cleans water.
strings.2-18.name: Ultrapure water
strings.2-18.hee1: Ultrapure water conducts electricity only as much as water itself splits into a tiny number of ions.
strings.2-19.name: Hydrogen peroxide
strings.2-19.hee1: Hydrogen peroxide came to be made by electrolysis too.
strings.2-20.name: Coal tar
strings.2-20.hee1: Bake coal without air, and you get coke, gas and black tar.
strings.2-21.name: Ammonia water
strings.2-21.hee1: Long ago, ammonia was a side product of gasworks.
strings.2-22.name: Aqua regia
strings.2-22.hee1: In 1940, to keep them from the Nazis, Hevesy dissolved the Nobel Prize medals of Laue and Franck in aqua regia and left them on a shelf. After the war the gold was taken out and the medals were made again.
strings.2-23.name: Wood distillation
strings.2-23.hee1: Neanderthals made tar from birch bark about 200,000 years ago (Campitello).
strings.2-24.name: Benzene
strings.2-24.hee1: In 1856 Perkin made mauve (the first synthetic dye) from tar, and the chemical industry began.
strings.2-25.name: Phenol
strings.2-25.hee1: Phenol, found in coal tar, was used to disinfect during surgery.
strings.2-26.name: Methanol
strings.2-26.hee1: Distill the liquid from baked wood and you get methanol (wood spirit).
strings.2-27.name: Formaldehyde
strings.2-27.hee1: Methanol is made to react with oxygen over a hot mesh of copper or silver.
strings.2-28.name: Phenolic resin
strings.2-28.hee1: The first synthetic plastic was made from phenol and formaldehyde.
strings.2-29.name: Rubber
strings.2-29.hee1: Put sulfur into rubber and heat it, and it becomes tough rubber that does not get sticky even when hot.
strings.2-30.name: Negative photoresist
strings.2-30.hee1: A material that hardens only where light hits it. It was used to copy the patterns of ICs.
strings.2-31.name: Films that harden in light: asphalt and dichromated gelatin
strings.2-31.hee1: The first photograph and the way ICs are made use the same idea.
strings.2-32.name: Positive photoresist
strings.2-32.hee1: A material that dissolves only where light hits it. It was first invented for paper used to copy drawings.
strings.2-33.name: Chemically amplified resist
strings.2-33.hee1: One acid made by light sets off hundreds of reactions. That is why a pattern can be copied with only a little light.
strings.2-35.name: Crude oil and distillation
strings.2-35.hee1: Crude oil is heated and split into gas, kerosene, heavy oil and more, by their different boiling temperatures.
strings.2-36.name: Ethylene
strings.2-36.hee1: Take the water out of alcohol and it becomes a gas called ethylene.
strings.2-37.name: Polyethylene
strings.2-37.hee1: Polyethylene was found by accident in an experiment using very high pressure.
strings.2-38.name: PTFE
strings.2-38.hee1: It was used in the Manhattan Project to handle UF6 (a corrosive gas).
strings.2-39.name: Ethanol
strings.2-39.hee1: Yeast is what makes alcoholic drinks. But even by distilling, you cannot get it stronger than 95.6%.
strings.2-40.name: Acetone
strings.2-40.hee1: Weizmann later became the first president of Israel.
strings.2-41.name: Epoxy resin
strings.2-41.hee1: The glue that sets hard when you mix two tubes together is epoxy.
strings.2-42.name: Acetic acid
strings.2-42.hee1: Pure acetic acid freezes like ice in a slightly cold room.
strings.2-43.name: Oil of vitriol
strings.2-43.hee1: Long ago, sulfuric acid was an "oil" made by roasting green crystals.
strings.2-44.name: Red phosphorus
strings.2-44.hee1: The striking strip on a matchbox is coated with red phosphorus.
strings.2-45.name: Light-curing resin
strings.2-45.hee1: The resin used to draw chip circuits and the resin in 3D printers work the same way.
strings.2-46.name: Transparent electrode ITO
strings.2-46.hee1: Indium got its name from the indigo color seen when the light of its flame was split apart.
strings.2-47.name: Chemically strengthened glass
strings.2-47.hee1: Push big atoms into small gaps, and the surface of the glass tightens up and becomes harder to break.
strings.2-48.name: CFC refrigerants
strings.2-48.hee1: CFCs were made to be safe, non-poisonous refrigerants, yet high in the sky they were destroying the ozone layer.
strings.2-49.name: Polyurethane foam insulation
strings.2-49.hee1: Inside the walls of a refrigerator is plastic packed full of tiny bubbles.
strings.2-50.name: Coordination polymerization catalyst
strings.2-50.hee1: The plastic in bottle caps is made by joining molecules one by one on a metal catalyst.
strings.2-51.name: Nylon
strings.2-51.hee1: On the day nylon stockings went on sale, thousands of people lined up at the stores.
strings.2-52.name: Boranes
strings.2-52.hee1: Diborane catches fire just from touching air, so chemists long ago built their own air-free equipment.
strings.2-53.name: Catalytic cracking
strings.2-53.hee1: Much of the gasoline for cars is made by breaking heavy crude oil apart over a catalyst.
strings.2-54.name: Chromatography
strings.2-54.hee1: The name chromatography means "color writing". At first it split plant pigments into bands of color.
strings.2-55.name: Conductive polymers
strings.2-55.hee1: Plastic that conducts electricity was born from a mistake in how much of a material was used in an experiment.
strings.2-56.name: Automatic glass-forming machines
strings.2-56.hee1: Glass bulbs for light bulbs came to be blown by machine, hundreds every minute.
strings.2-57.name: Diazonaphthoquinone
strings.2-57.hee1: A powder that breaks down when light hits it became the "eye" that copies IC patterns.
strings.2-58.name: Acetic anhydride
strings.2-58.hee1: Take one water out of two acetic acids, and you get something that reacts much more easily.
strings.2-59.name: Cinnamic acid
strings.2-59.hee1: A relative of the smell of cinnamon that joins together in light.
strings.2-60.name: Polyvinyl alcohol
strings.2-60.hee1: The stuff in laundry starch can be made from gas.
strings.2-61.name: Polyvinyl cinnamate
strings.2-61.hee1: It hardens only where the light hits.
strings.2-62.name: Hazard labels
strings.2-62.hee1: The four-digit number on the back of a truck is a UN number that means the same thing anywhere in the world.
strings.2-63.name: Zylon
strings.2-63.hee1: A very tough fiber, even used for the parachute cords of a Mars probe.
strings.2-64.name: Fluororubber
strings.2-64.hee1: A relative of the Teflon on frying pans. Rubber made strong against heat and oil by the power of fluorine.
strings.2-65.name: Linseed oil and varnish
strings.2-65.hee1: Cloth soaked in linseed oil can catch fire by itself.
strings.2-66.name: Soot and printing ink
strings.2-66.hee1: Printing ink is oil, not water, so the metal type does not repel it.
strings.3-01.name: Campfire
strings.3-01.hee1: The heat of a campfire escapes all around.
strings.3-02.name: Hearth stove
strings.3-02.hee1: Surround a fire with walls and the heat bounces back, making it hotter than a campfire.
strings.3-04.name: Bellows
strings.3-04.hee1: Blowing air makes a fire hotter. The name of Japan's tatara furnace comes from these bellows.
strings.3-05.name: Blast furnace (the game's vanilla blast furnace)
strings.3-05.hee1: In a tall furnace that burns coke with a strong blast of air, iron flows out as a liquid.
strings.3-06.name: Reverberatory furnace
strings.3-06.hee1: When ore is roasted, sulfur goes off as smoke. It used to be poison smoke, but if you collect it, it becomes sulfuric acid.
strings.3-07.name: Crucible furnace
strings.3-07.hee1: Melt things inside a crucible, and the fuel and flames do not dirty what is inside.
strings.3-08.name: Converter
strings.3-08.hee1: Just blowing air into melted iron makes it hotter, with no fuel at all.
strings.3-09.name: Thermocouple
strings.3-09.hee1: Before that, in 1782, Wedgwood measured kiln temperature by how much clay shrank.
strings.3-10.name: Acheson furnace
strings.3-10.hee1: Bake charcoal with electricity far too much, and it turns into graphite.
strings.3-11.name: Optical pyrometer
strings.3-11.hee1: It measures temperature by comparing the color of a hot thing with the color of a light bulb filament.
strings.3-12.name: Firebrick
strings.3-12.hee1: Ordinary bricks melt in a furnace. Only bricks with lots of quartz can take it.
strings.3-13.name: Thermal insulation
strings.3-13.hee1: Diatomaceous earth is soil full of tiny holes, made from piled-up shells of tiny living things.
strings.3-14.name: Induction furnace
strings.3-14.hee1: The same idea as an induction (IH) cooktop.
strings.3-15.name: Arc furnace
strings.3-15.hee1: An electric spark (arc) makes heat of over 2000°C.
strings.3-16.name: Vacuum furnace
strings.3-16.hee1: Pump out the air and then heat things, and they bake without rusting.
strings.3-18.name: Regenerative furnace (equipment)
strings.3-18.hee1: A furnace that uses the heat of the exhaust gas, which would be thrown away, to warm up the next air.
strings.3-19.name: By-product coke oven
strings.3-19.hee1: Old coke ovens burned off their gas and tar and threw them away.
strings.3-20.name: Fireclay
strings.3-20.hee1: Since long ago, crucibles and the insides of furnaces have been made of clay that stands up to heat.
strings.3-21.name: Heat pipe
strings.3-21.hee1: Inside is a vacuum with only a little water, so the water boils even at about body temperature and carries heat.
strings.3-22.name: Vapor-compression refrigeration cycle
strings.3-22.hee1: A refrigerator is not a machine that makes cold; it is a "heat pump" that pumps the heat inside out.
strings.3-23.name: Heat pump
strings.3-23.hee1: An air conditioner's heating collects heat even from the cold winter air outside and carries it into the room.
strings.3-24.name: Heating wire heater
strings.3-24.hee1: The glowing red wires in a toaster are made of a special metal of nickel mixed with chromium, so they do not burn out even when red hot.
strings.3-25.name: Calcium carbide
strings.3-25.hee1: Carbide was found in a failed try at making aluminum.
strings.3-26.name: Sintered alumina ceramics
strings.3-26.hee1: The white part of a spark plug is baked alumina.
strings.4-01.name: Water-wheel generator
strings.4-01.hee1: The more water flows and the higher it falls, the more electricity you can make.
strings.4-02.name: Steam engine
strings.4-02.hee1: The first steam engines were for pumping water out of coal mines.
strings.4-03.name: Copper cable
strings.4-03.hee1: Some of the electricity flowing through a wire is lost as heat. Thick wires and high voltage cut the loss.
strings.4-04.name: Dynamo and natural magnets
strings.4-04.hee1: Spin a coil near a magnet and electricity is made.
strings.4-05.name: Self-excited dynamo
strings.4-05.hee1: It can make electricity without a magnet.
strings.4-06.name: Steam turbine
strings.4-06.hee1: Steam spins a bladed wheel fast. Because it spins so fast, it is the best fit for making electricity.
strings.4-07.name: Lead-acid battery
strings.4-07.hee1: The same as a car battery.
strings.4-08.name: Electric motor
strings.4-08.hee1: A motor is a generator in reverse. Send electricity through it and it spins.
strings.4-09.name: High-frequency oscillator
strings.4-09.hee1: The machines that made transistors ran on vacuum tubes.
strings.4-10.name: Transformer
strings.4-10.hee1: With alternating current, you can raise or lower the voltage. Sending power at high voltage loses less electricity.
strings.4-11.name: Rectifier
strings.4-11.hee1: It turns AC into DC. Electrolysis needs DC.
strings.4-12.name: Electric furnace
strings.4-12.hee1: Even without nichrome, you can make a heating element from a graphite rod.
strings.4-13.name: Voltaic pile
strings.4-13.hee1: The first battery was a stack of copper and zinc disks with salt-water-soaked cloth between them.
strings.4-14.name: Steam power generation
strings.4-14.hee1: In 1882, electricity made with steam became a town's lights for the first time.
strings.4-15.name: Lithium-ion battery
strings.4-15.hee1: Charging means tucking lithium ions into the gaps in graphite.
strings.4-16.name: Arc lamp
strings.4-16.hee1: Electric light began with "sparks", before the light bulb.
strings.4-17.name: Stepper motor
strings.4-17.hee1: Each time you send it a pulse of electricity, it clicks around by exactly a set angle.
strings.4-18.name: Electric fan
strings.4-18.hee1: The first electric fan was just a motor with a propeller on it.
strings.4-19.name: Switching power supply
strings.4-19.hee1: Phone chargers are small because they switch the electricity on and off tens of thousands of times a second, which lets the transformer be small.
strings.4-20.name: Vibration motor
strings.4-20.hee1: The weight is fixed to one side only, so when it spins the whole thing shakes.
strings.4-21.name: Brushless DC motor
strings.4-21.hee1: The motors in computer fans and air conditioners have no parts that rub and wear out.
strings.4-22.name: Induction motor
strings.4-22.hee1: No wires are connected to the spinning part of an induction motor, yet it turns, pulled along by an invisible "spinning magnet".
strings.4-23.name: Cross-flow fan
strings.4-23.hee1: Inside an air conditioner's indoor unit is a long, thin fan wheel shaped like a tube (a chikuwa), which blows out a wide sheet of air.
strings.4-24.name: Bladeless fan
strings.4-24.hee1: A bladeless fan really has blades inside its base, and the air coming out of the ring pulls the air around it along, making the flow many times bigger.
strings.4-25.name: Regenerative braking
strings.4-25.hee1: When an electric car brakes, it can charge its battery a little with the electricity made at that moment.
strings.4-26.name: EV fast charging
strings.4-26.hee1: In fast charging, the charger and the car talk to each other and decide "this much current right now".
strings.4-27.name: Induction coil
strings.4-27.hee1: From a single battery it can make lightning-like sparks of tens of thousands of volts.
strings.4-28.name: Dry cell battery
strings.4-28.hee1: Even a "dry" cell is not completely dry inside; it holds a damp paste.
strings.4-29.name: Gas turbines and jet engines
strings.4-29.hee1: The big fan at the front of an airliner's engine is turned by the turbine at the back.
strings.4-30.name: Three-phase AC transmission
strings.4-30.hee1: The wires on utility poles come in sets of three because they carry three-phase AC.
strings.4-31.name: Nuclear power
strings.4-31.hee1: The first nuclear power lit up four light bulbs ⚠️
strings.4-32.name: High-voltage direct current transmission
strings.4-32.hee1: When sending electricity a long way through cables on the sea floor, direct current wastes less than alternating current.
strings.4-33.name: Water turbine
strings.4-33.hee1: The wheel in a hydroelectric plant is not an old wooden water wheel but a turbine with metal blades.
strings.4-34.name: AC generator
strings.4-34.hee1: Every power station generator is one of these. The voltage flips back and forth 50 times a second (eastern Japan) or 60 times (western Japan).
strings.4-35.name: High-voltage transmission
strings.4-35.hee1: Power lines sit on tall towers because the higher the voltage, the more easily it jumps through the air, so it must be kept far from the ground.
strings.4-36.name: Daniell cell
strings.4-36.hee1: Splitting the liquid into two kept the battery's power from dropping.
strings.4-37.name: NaS battery
strings.4-37.hee1: A battery whose insides are melted and piping hot. Kept at 300°C, it works as a piggy bank for electricity.
strings.5-01.name: Hand piston pump
strings.5-01.hee1: Because of the weight of the air, even horses cannot pull them apart.
strings.5-02.name: Vacuum tube
strings.5-02.hee1: Before transistors, signals were made bigger with parts that looked like glass light bulbs.
strings.5-03.name: Mercury column and pressure units
strings.5-03.hee1: The "hPa (hectopascal)" in weather forecasts is named after Pascal.
strings.5-04.name: Rotary vane oil pump
strings.5-04.hee1: The "hummm" sound in a lab is this pump.
strings.5-05.name: Mercury diffusion pump
strings.5-05.hee1: It has no moving parts, yet it blows the air away with a wind of vapor.
strings.5-06.name: Oil diffusion pump
strings.5-06.hee1: Instead of mercury, it uses a special oil that hardly evaporates at all.
strings.5-07.name: Turbomolecular pump
strings.5-07.hee1: The tips of its blades spin at nearly the speed of sound.
strings.5-08.name: Ion pump
strings.5-08.hee1: Instead of pushing the air out, it traps it inside metal.
strings.5-09.name: Cryopump → liquid nitrogen cold trap
strings.5-09.hee1: It freezes the air and sticks it to the wall.
strings.5-10.name: Vacuum gauge
strings.5-10.hee1: It measures the "nothingness" of empty space by how fast a wire cools down.
strings.5-11.name: Vacuum chamber
strings.5-11.hee1: Gas seeps out even from the metal walls, so they are baked to drive it out.
strings.5-12.name: Vacuum seal
strings.5-12.hee1: The wires at the base of a light bulb are a special metal that stretches and shrinks exactly as much as glass does.
strings.5-14.name: Vacuum deposition
strings.5-14.hee1: The silver inside a potato chip bag is also aluminum put on by vacuum deposition.
strings.5-15.name: Sprengel mercury pump
strings.5-15.hee1: The vacuum in light bulbs was made with drops of mercury.
strings.5-16.name: Getter
strings.5-16.hee1: The silver patch in a vacuum tube is the mark left after it "ate" the leftover air.
strings.6-01.name: Electrolyzer
strings.6-01.hee1: Pure water hardly conducts electricity at all.
strings.6-02.name: Gas holder
strings.6-02.hee1: 1) Gas tanks in the gas-lamp era used water as their lid. 2) The pressure is the weight of the bell ÷ its area. 3) At King's Cross in London the frames still stand, now part of parks and homes. 4) Hydrogen escapes even through the gaps in metal.
strings.6-03.name: Compressor
strings.6-03.hee1: In the 1880s high-pressure cylinders were made, and gases could be carried around.
strings.6-04.name: Rock salt mine
strings.6-04.hee1: Rock salt is "a sea that turned to stone".
strings.6-05.name: Chlor-alkali electrolysis
strings.6-05.hee1: Salt gives chlorine and caustic soda at the same time.
strings.6-06.name: Hydrochloric acid
strings.6-06.hee1: Burn hydrogen in chlorine and you get hydrogen chloride; dissolve it in water and you get hydrochloric acid.
strings.6-07.name: Air separation
strings.6-07.hee1: Turn air into a liquid and "distill" it.
strings.6-08.name: Noble gas purification
strings.6-08.hee1: Most of the gas in an excimer laser is neon.
strings.6-09.name: Haber-Bosch process
strings.6-09.hee1: The catalyst is made from magnetite.
strings.6-10.name: Saltpeter bed
strings.6-11.name: Nitric acid
strings.6-11.hee1: Pour sulfuric acid on saltpeter, and nitric acid comes out.
strings.6-12.name: Lead chamber process sulfuric acid
strings.6-12.hee1: Why sulfuric acid factories were made of lead.
strings.6-13.name: Contact process sulfuric acid
strings.6-13.hee1: With a catalyst such as platinum, you can make very strong sulfuric acid.
strings.6-14.name: Fluorine gas
strings.6-14.hee1: Fluorine is the "most dangerous element": many chemists were poisoned before it was finally separated out.
strings.6-15.name: Helium (avoided)
strings.6-15.hee1: Helium was found on the Sun first (from the light of the 1868 eclipse). On Earth we can only get the helium that piled up underground from radioactive decay.
strings.6-16.name: Collecting natural saltpeter
strings.6-16.hee1: An ingredient of gunpowder was taken from the soil of old animal sheds.
strings.7-01.name: Optical glass
strings.7-01.hee1: Put lead in glass and it sparkles (crystal glass).
strings.7-02.name: Fused quartz
strings.7-02.hee1: Burn hydrogen and oxygen together and it gets hot enough to melt quartz.
strings.7-03.name: Lens grinding
strings.7-03.hee1: Lenses are polished not with hard tools, but with soft pitch.
strings.7-04.name: Refracting telescope and achromatic lens
strings.7-04.hee1: Glue two kinds of glass together, and the rainbow-colored blur disappears.
strings.7-05.name: Reflecting mirror
strings.7-05.hee1: Silver mirrors are made by a chemical reaction that coats the glass with silver from a liquid with silver dissolved in it.
strings.7-06.name: Prism spectroscopy
strings.7-06.hee1: Split light into a rainbow, and you can tell what the stars are made of.
strings.7-07.name: Diffraction grating
strings.7-07.hee1: The rainbow colors on the back of a CD come from a diffraction grating too.
strings.7-09.name: Interferometer
strings.7-09.hee1: Use light waves as a ruler, and you can measure one hundredth of a hair.
strings.7-10.name: Mercury lamp
strings.7-10.hee1: Semiconductor factories have yellow light because it is a color the resist does not react to.
strings.7-11.name: Silver halide photomask
strings.7-11.hee1: The circuit patterns of the first ICs were made by cutting film by hand.
strings.7-12.name: Chrome mask
strings.7-12.hee1: The "master copy" of a circuit is a shadow picture made of thin metal on clear quartz.
strings.7-13.name: Laser principle
strings.7-13.hee1: The first laser shone using a ruby gemstone.
strings.7-14.name: CO2 laser
strings.7-14.hee1: This laser's light cannot pass through glass, so its windows are made of salt crystals.
strings.7-15.name: Ultraviolet optical materials
strings.7-15.hee1: Natural fluorite becomes the window of cutting-edge lasers.
strings.7-16.name: Immersion optics
strings.7-16.hee1: Just putting water between the lens and the wafer lets you draw finer patterns.
strings.7-17.name: Multilayer mirror
strings.7-17.hee1: Light that one layer cannot reflect is bounced back by stacking 40 weak reflections.
strings.7-18.name: EUV light source
strings.7-18.hee1: Falling droplets of tin are shot with a laser to make them glow.
strings.7-19.name: Projection lens
strings.7-19.hee1: The lens of a lithography machine is a "tower of glass" stacking dozens of lenses.
strings.7-20.name: Excimer laser
strings.7-20.hee1: "Excimer" means "a pair that sticks together only when excited".
strings.7-21.name: Ultra-low expansion glass
strings.7-21.hee1: Glass whose length hardly changes whether you heat it or cool it.
strings.7-22.name: Anti-reflection coating
strings.7-22.hee1: Stack thin films on glass, and the glass becomes "invisible".
strings.7-23.name: LiDAR
strings.7-23.hee1: Apollo 15 studied the bumps of the Moon by timing how long laser light took to bounce back from its surface.
strings.7-24.name: Camera autofocus
strings.7-24.hee1: The first mass-produced "camera that focuses by itself" was made by Konica of Japan, in 1977.
strings.7-25.name: Semiconductor laser
strings.7-25.hee1: The light running through optical fibers comes from semiconductor lasers smaller than a grain of rice.
strings.7-26.name: Holography
strings.7-26.hee1: The shiny patterns on banknotes and cards are holograms, which record a whole light wave.
strings.7-27.name: Petzval lens
strings.7-27.hee1: Before this lens, you had to sit still for minutes while your photo was taken.
strings.7-28.name: Free-electron laser
strings.7-28.hee1: A laser that lets you choose the color of light just by changing the speed of the electrons.
strings.8-01.name: Lathe
strings.8-01.hee1: A lathe that moves the cutter with a lead screw took away the shaking of human hands.
strings.8-02.name: Screw cutting and interchangeable parts
strings.8-02.hee1: Screws from any shop fit because the angle of the thread is fixed by a standard.
strings.8-03.name: Flat surfaces and surface plates
strings.8-03.hee1: The way to make "perfectly flat" out of nothing is to rub three plates against each other.
strings.8-04.name: Calipers and micrometers
strings.8-04.hee1: If you know how many mm a screw moves in one turn, you can measure 0.01 mm.
strings.8-05.name: Gauge block
strings.8-05.hee1: Metal pieces that are flat enough stick together without any glue.
strings.8-06.name: Interferometric length measurement
strings.8-06.hee1: The definition of one meter changed from a metal bar to light.
strings.8-07.name: Vibration isolation and constant temperature
strings.8-07.hee1: In a precision factory, work stops just because a truck drives past.
strings.8-08.name: Ball-screw precision stage
strings.8-08.hee1: Little steel balls roll inside the groove of the screw.
strings.8-09.name: Linear motor and air bearing stage
strings.8-09.hee1: The stage of a lithography machine speeds up like a roller coaster and stops to the nanometer.
strings.8-10.name: Optical microscope
strings.8-10.hee1: With a light microscope, you cannot see things smaller than the wavelength of light.
strings.8-11.name: Electron microscope
strings.8-11.hee1: Use electrons instead of "light", and you can see even viruses.
strings.8-12.name: Ruling engine
strings.8-12.hee1: If the temperature changed during the days of ruling lines, the work was ruined.
strings.8-13.name: Droplet generator
strings.8-13.hee1: EUV light sources and inkjet printers are relatives.
strings.8-14.name: Precision lens barrel assembly
strings.8-14.hee1: Even the best lens blurs if it is put together 0.001 mm off.
strings.8-15.name: Quartz crystal oscillator
strings.8-15.hee1: Inside a wristwatch, a quartz crystal shakes 32768 times a second.
strings.8-16.name: Scanning probe microscope
strings.8-16.hee1: It sees the bumps of single atoms by tracing them with a sharp needle.
strings.8-17.name: Alignment
strings.8-17.hee1: Dozens of transparent pictures are stacked with only a few ten-thousandths of a hair's width of slip.
strings.8-18.name: Synthetic quartz
strings.8-18.hee1: Almost all the quartz in watches is artificial crystal grown inside a pressure cooker.
strings.8-19.name: Pulley
strings.8-19.hee1: You need only a quarter of the force, but you pull the rope four times as far.
strings.8-20.name: Ball bearing
strings.8-20.hee1: Put steel balls in between, and things roll instead of rubbing. That is why wheels and motors turn so easily.
strings.8-21.name: Sextant
strings.8-21.hee1: Line up the Sun with the horizon using two mirrors, and you can tell where on Earth you are.
strings.8-22.name: Meter prototype
strings.8-22.hee1: One meter was a length decided from the size of the Earth.
strings.8-23.name: International Prototype of the Kilogram
strings.8-23.hee1: Until 2019, one kilogram was the weight of a single lump of metal in a vault in Paris.
strings.8-24.name: International System of Units (SI)
strings.8-24.hee1: The whole world can use the same "1 meter" and "1 second" thanks to the SI, decided in 1960.
strings.8-25.name: Watt balance
strings.8-25.hee1: Today one kilogram is set not by a lump of metal but by electric force.
strings.8-26.name: Typewriter
strings.8-26.hee1: The keys on a computer are still in the same order as on typewriters 150 years ago.
strings.8-27.name: Strain wave gearing
strings.8-27.hee1: Inside a robot's joints, a ring of metal gear teeth turns while bending into a wobbly oval.
strings.8-28.name: Strain gauge
strings.8-28.hee1: The strain gauge was thought up by a researcher studying how water tanks shake in earthquakes.
strings.8-29.name: Roller chain
strings.8-29.hee1: The shape of a bicycle chain has hardly changed from the design thought up more than 140 years ago.
strings.8-30.name: Atomic clock
strings.8-30.hee1: Today one second is defined as the time it takes a cesium atom to vibrate 9,192,631,770 times.
strings.8-31.name: Grinding machine
strings.8-31.hee1: Even steel too hard to cut with a blade can be shaped to one hundredth of a hair's width by rubbing it with a grinding wheel.
strings.8-32.name: Gear cutting machine
strings.8-32.hee1: Accuracy went up by remaking the gears of the gear-making machine more exactly, over and over.
strings.8-33.name: Mass spectrometry
strings.8-33.hee1: Bend atoms with an electromagnet and they fly apart, sorted by weight.
strings.8-34.name: NC
strings.8-34.hee1: The first NC machine tool moved its cutter by reading paper tape with holes punched in it.
strings.8-35.name: Quartz wristwatch
strings.8-35.hee1: The quartz crystal inside a quartz watch shakes as many as 32768 times a second.
strings.8-36.name: Tilting-pad thrust bearing
strings.8-36.hee1: The hundreds of tons of a big water turbine float on just a thin film of oil.
strings.8-37.name: Electrical discharge machining
strings.8-37.hee1: Tens of thousands of sparks a second melt and carve away hard metal bit by bit.
strings.8-38.name: Cryo-electron microscope
strings.8-38.hee1: Freeze water in an instant, and no ice crystals form; it sets solid like glass.
strings.8-39.name: Arc welding
strings.8-39.hee1: The light from arc welding is so strong that welders protect their eyes with a dark mask.
strings.8-40.name: Gas welding and cutting
strings.8-40.hee1: An oxygen-acetylene flame is about 3100°C and cuts iron like butter ⚠️
strings.8-41.name: Hydraulic forging press
strings.8-41.hee1: A 50,000-ton press is as big as a building several stories tall ⚠️
strings.8-42.name: Dividing engine
strings.8-42.hee1: The scale marks on a sextant came to be cut by a machine instead of by hand.
strings.8-43.name: Mechanical clock and gear train
strings.8-43.hee1: The hands of a clock turn at exactly the right speed because of the ratio of the numbers of gear teeth.
strings.8-44.name: Mainspring
strings.8-44.hee1: A clock's mainspring is a strip of steel that coils up when you wind it and gives out power as it unwinds.
strings.8-45.name: Balance wheel and hairspring
strings.8-45.hee1: The little wheel inside a wristwatch swings back and forth several times every second.
strings.8-46.name: Lever escapement
strings.8-46.hee1: The tick-tock sound is the escapement letting the gear go one tooth at a time.
strings.8-47.name: Jewel bearings
strings.8-47.hee1: "17 jewels" means there are 17 rubies inside the watch.
strings.8-48.name: Automatic winding
strings.8-48.hee1: Swing your arm, and a weight inside turns and winds the mainspring.
strings.9-01.name: Ge zone refining
strings.9-01.hee1: Pass a melted band through many times, and the dirt gathers at one end.
strings.9-02.name: Zone leveling
strings.9-02.hee1: Moving the melted band back and forth spreads the added impurity evenly through the whole bar.
strings.9-03.name: Point-contact transistor
strings.9-03.hee1: Two gold contacts were pressed onto germanium with a plastic wedge.
strings.9-04.name: Alloy-junction transistor
strings.9-04.hee1: Put a bead of indium on each side of germanium and bake it, and you get a three-layer part.
strings.9-05.name: Ge diode
strings.9-05.hee1: A part with a thin needle standing on germanium caught radar waves.
strings.9-06.name: Oxide etching
strings.9-06.hee1: When the oxide film is all dissolved, the surface repels water, so you can see with your eyes when it is done.
strings.9-07.name: Ge single-crystal pulling
strings.9-07.hee1: Inside the company, people objected: "We don't need single crystals."
strings.9-08.name: CZ process
strings.9-08.hee1: Most of the world's silicon is made with a method born from an accident 100 years ago.
strings.9-09.name: FZ method
strings.9-09.hee1: With no crucible, the liquid silicon floats, held up by surface tension alone.
strings.9-10.name: Grown-junction transistor
strings.9-10.hee1: Materials were mixed in while the crystal was growing, making 3 layers inside.
strings.9-11.name: Dopant sources
strings.9-11.hee1: Arsenic is a poison, but it is also inside the transistors in your smartphone.
strings.9-12.name: Wafer slicing
strings.9-12.hee1: When wafers are sliced, a good part of them turns into dust and is lost.
strings.9-13.name: Lapping and mirror polishing
strings.9-13.hee1: The bumps on a wafer polished like a mirror are only a few dozen atoms high.
strings.9-14.name: RCA clean
strings.9-14.hee1: A recipe from more than 50 years ago is still the basic one in today's most advanced factories.
strings.9-15.name: Thermal oxidation
strings.9-15.hee1: Silicon's own "rust" turns into glass and protects it.
strings.9-16.name: Thermal diffusion
strings.9-16.hee1: Bake at 1000°C for hours, and atoms walk little by little through the solid.
strings.9-17.name: Mesa transistor
strings.9-17.hee1: "Mesa" means table in Spanish. It is the shape of the flat-topped hills of the American West.
strings.9-18.name: Planar process
strings.9-18.hee1: The idea of "making it while keeping it flat" was the start of the IC.
strings.9-19.name: Resist coating
strings.9-19.hee1: It is just like spinning pizza dough to spread it out.
strings.9-20.name: Contact and proximity printing
strings.9-20.hee1: The first ICs were made by printing the shadow of a mask, like a shadow picture.
strings.9-21.name: Development and post-bake
strings.9-21.hee1: The circuit is brought out with the same steps as developing a photograph.
strings.9-22.name: Integrated circuit
strings.9-22.hee1: The first IC was one transistor and a few parts, about the size of a fingertip.
strings.9-23.name: MOSFET
strings.9-23.hee1: Of all the things humans have ever made, the MOSFET is the most numerous.
strings.9-24.name: CMOS
strings.9-24.hee1: The batteries in calculators and watches last for years thanks to CMOS.
strings.9-25.name: Metal wiring
strings.9-25.hee1: The wires inside a chip are the same metal as aluminum foil.
strings.9-26.name: Sputtering
strings.9-26.hee1: Making films by playing billiards with atoms.
strings.9-27.name: Dry etching
strings.9-27.hee1: Dissolving with liquid also eats sideways, so an electric discharge is used to carve straight down only.
strings.9-28.name: Ion implantation
strings.9-28.hee1: Atoms are used as bullets and shot to exactly the right depth.
strings.9-29.name: Annealing
strings.9-29.hee1: Just like annealing metal, heat lets the atoms line up again.
strings.9-30.name: Epitaxy and CVD
strings.9-30.hee1: The reaction that fattens rods in the Siemens process is used to make thin films.
strings.9-31.name: CMP
strings.9-31.hee1: Like building a skyscraper of dozens of floors, flattening each floor as you go.
strings.9-32.name: Dicing
strings.9-32.hee1: Hundreds of chips are cut out of a single wafer.
strings.9-33.name: Wire bonding
strings.9-33.hee1: The wire joining the chip to the outside is gold, about a third as thick as a hair.
strings.9-34.name: Encapsulation
strings.9-34.hee1: The black outside of a chip is plastic, like a shell protecting it from moisture.
strings.9-35.name: Testing
strings.9-35.hee1: Not every chip that is made actually works.
strings.9-36.name: Copper interconnects
strings.9-36.hee1: The name of the inlay work of Damascus is used for the most advanced wiring.
strings.9-37.name: FinFET
strings.9-37.hee1: The transistor went from a one-story house to a "standing plate".
strings.9-38.name: GAA
strings.9-38.hee1: In the end, the gate wraps all the way around the channel.
strings.9-39.name: Reduction projection lithography
strings.9-39.hee1: The history of semiconductors is a history of "shorter light, finer patterns".
strings.9-40.name: EUV lithography machine
strings.9-40.hee1: A "camera" bigger than a house that only one company in the world can make.
strings.9-41.name: Power semiconductors and inverters
strings.9-41.hee1: An electric car switches electricity on and off thousands of times a second to turn its motor.
strings.9-42.name: Image sensor
strings.9-42.hee1: Phone cameras and optical mice both have the same family of chip inside, one that "turns light into electrons and counts them".
strings.9-43.name: MEMS
strings.9-43.hee1: Inside a smartphone are tiny springs and weights made of silicon, and they really move when you tilt it.
strings.9-44.name: Thermistor
strings.9-44.hee1: An air conditioner's thermometer is a tiny ceramic bead that lets electricity through more easily as it warms up.
strings.9-45.name: Bayer color filter
strings.9-45.hee1: Half of a camera's pixels are green, because the human eye is most sensitive to green.
strings.9-46.name: Sensors that detect people
strings.9-46.hee1: A motion sensor does not sense "the shape of a person" but "changes" in the infrared coming from your body, so the light may go off if you stay still.
strings.9-47.name: Particle accelerator
strings.9-47.hee1: Semiconductor factories have rows of small accelerators (ion implanters).
strings.9-48.name: Semiconductor heterostructure
strings.9-48.hee1: The lasers in CDs and optical fibers shine inside a sandwich of different semiconductors stacked in layers only atoms thick.
strings.9-49.name: Thyristor
strings.9-49.hee1: The devices that change the speed of train motors were first made with semiconductor switches called thyristors.
strings.10-01.name: Electromagnet
strings.10-01.hee1: A magnet that turns back into plain iron when you switch it off.
strings.10-02.name: Relay
strings.10-02.hee1: A small clicking switch is the ancestor of the computer.
strings.10-03.name: Telegraph
strings.10-03.hee1: Thanks to the telegraph, news that took days by horse arrived in an instant.
strings.10-04.name: Feedback control
strings.10-04.hee1: Look at the gap from the target and fix it: that is the basis of all automatic control.
strings.10-05.name: Boolean algebra and switching circuits
strings.10-06.name: Relay computer
strings.10-06.hee1: The first programmable computer was a bunch of clattering switches.
strings.10-07.name: Vacuum tube flip-flops and computers
strings.10-07.hee1: ENIAC's vacuum tubes burned out all the time, and were replaced every day.
strings.10-08.name: Magnetic-core memory
strings.10-08.hee1: The memory of old computers was a hand-woven net of tiny magnets.
strings.10-09.name: Transistor logic
strings.10-09.hee1: Computers that filled a room shrank to about the size of a desk.
strings.10-10.name: IC logic
strings.10-10.hee1: The computer that went to the Moon lined up thousands of small ICs, all the same kind.
strings.10-11.name: Adders, counters and registers
strings.10-11.hee1: Adding is just passing the "carry" to the next digit.
strings.10-12.name: DRAM
strings.10-12.hee1: Electricity stored in a tiny capacitor is a "1". Leave it alone and it leaks away and is forgotten.
strings.10-13.name: Microprocessor
strings.10-13.hee1: The world's first microprocessor was born for a Japanese calculator.
strings.10-14.name: Microcomputer
strings.10-14.hee1: Rice cookers and washing machines have small computers inside too.
strings.10-15.name: Lithography machine control
strings.10-15.hee1: The machines that make chips are run by those very chips.
strings.10-16.name: Neural network
strings.10-16.hee1: Starting from stone and sand, we arrived at a machine that can read numbers.
strings.10-17.name: CAD
strings.10-17.hee1: Keep drawings as numbers instead of on paper, and you can fix them as many times as you like.
strings.10-18.name: Compiler
strings.10-18.hee1: "I want to give a computer orders in human words" was the start of programming languages.
strings.10-19.name: VLSI design methodology
strings.10-19.hee1: Even millions of transistors can be designed if you lay them out by fixed rules.
strings.10-20.name: Analytical Engine
strings.10-20.hee1: In an age without electricity, a computer that ran programs with nothing but gears was designed.
strings.10-21.name: Slide rule
strings.10-21.hee1: A ruler that turns multiplication into "adding lengths". Until the calculator came along, engineers always had one in their pocket.
strings.10-22.name: Keyboard
strings.10-22.hee1: Inside a keyboard is a small computer that checks which keys are pressed.
strings.10-23.name: Flash memory
strings.10-23.hee1: Electrons are shut inside a thin glass wall, so it remembers for years even with the power off.
strings.10-24.name: SSD
strings.10-24.hee1: The tiny computer inside an SSD quietly spreads out where it writes, so the same spot does not wear out from being written over and over.
strings.10-25.name: GPU
strings.10-25.hee1: A GPU lines up thousands of small calculators that can only do simple math, and runs them all at once.
strings.10-26.name: Industrial robot
strings.10-26.hee1: The first robot to work in a factory had the job of taking out hot metal parts that were dangerous for people to touch.
strings.10-27.name: Servomechanism
strings.10-27.hee1: "Servo" comes from a French word meaning "to obey", and at first it was the name of a device that turned a ship's rudder.
strings.10-28.name: Reinforcement learning
strings.10-28.hee1: Without being taught the rules of a game, an AI got good just by watching the screen and the score and playing again and again.
strings.10-29.name: Transformer and large AI
strings.10-29.hee1: The T in "GPT", often part of the names of chat AIs, is the T of this Transformer.
strings.10-30.name: SLAM (finding your place and making a map at the same time)
strings.10-30.hee1: A robot vacuum works out "Where am I?" and "What shape is the room?" bit by bit, with the same calculation.
strings.10-31.name: Stored-program computer
strings.10-31.hee1: The first stored-program computer remembered numbers as dots on a CRT screen, like a TV.
strings.10-32.name: Floating-point standard
strings.10-32.hee1: When a computer works out 0.1 + 0.2, the answer can be just a tiny bit off from 0.3.
strings.10-33.name: Hard disk drive
strings.10-33.hee1: The first hard disk stacked up 50 disks about 60 cm across, and held only about 5 MB.
strings.10-34.name: Operating system
strings.10-34.hee1: The ideas of UNIX from more than 50 years ago still live on inside smartphones.
strings.10-35.name: Circuit simulator
strings.10-35.hee1: Before a chip is made, it is run many times inside a computer to check it.
strings.10-36.name: RISC
strings.10-36.hee1: Smartphone CPUs are descendants of a design that made the instructions simple on purpose, to be faster.
strings.10-37.name: Predicting protein shapes with AI
strings.10-37.hee1: AI can now guess how a protein folds up just from the order of its amino acids.
strings.10-38.name: Storage-tube graphics terminal
strings.10-38.hee1: To erase lines, this screen flashed the whole display bright and wiped everything at once.
strings.10-39.name: Small BASIC microcontroller board
strings.10-39.hee1: A "stamp" is a postage stamp. A computer about as small as a stamp.
strings.11-01.name: Irrigation
strings.11-01.hee1: Too much watering ruins a field with salt.
strings.11-02.name: Plow
strings.11-02.hee1: The steel plow turned the great prairies of North America into farmland.
strings.11-03.name: Crop rotation
strings.11-03.hee1: Growing beans makes the field richer.
strings.11-04.name: Plant breeding
strings.11-04.hee1: Genetics began with peas in a monastery garden.
strings.11-05.name: Compost
strings.11-05.hee1: Tiny creatures that eat fallen leaves make fertilizer.
strings.11-06.name: Superphosphate
strings.11-06.hee1: Dissolve bones in sulfuric acid and they become fertilizer.
strings.11-07.name: Nitrogen fertilizer
strings.11-07.hee1: Nitrogen from the air becomes bread.
strings.11-08.name: Milling
strings.11-08.hee1: Grinding flour was one of the first jobs people handed over to machines.
strings.11-09.name: Bread
strings.11-09.hee1: The holes in bread are yeast farts (CO2).
strings.11-10.name: Alcohol and vinegar
strings.11-10.hee1: Leave alcohol out in the air and it turns into vinegar.
strings.11-11.name: Salting, drying and smoking
strings.11-11.hee1: Salt was once called "white gold", and it is said to be where the word salary comes from ⚠️
strings.11-12.name: Canning
strings.11-12.hee1: For about 50 years after cans were invented, there was no can opener ⚠️
strings.11-13.name: Refrigeration and freezing
strings.11-13.hee1: The refrigerator and liquid air were made by the same person.
strings.11-14.name: Sugar
strings.11-14.hee1: White sugar is brown juice made white with charcoal.
strings.11-15.name: Pasteurization
strings.11-15.hee1: The word "pasteurized" on milk cartons comes from Pasteur's name.
strings.11-16.name: Bordeaux mixture
strings.11-16.hee1: A blue spray put on grapes by the road to stop thieves turned out to stop disease too.
strings.11-17.name: Espresso pressure brewing
strings.11-17.hee1: Espresso is made by pushing hot water through coffee grounds at about 9 atmospheres, about 4 times the pressure in a tire.
strings.12-01.name: Roman concrete
strings.12-01.hee1: Roman concrete from 2000 years ago actually gets stronger in seawater ⚠️
strings.12-02.name: Portland cement
strings.12-02.hee1: It got its name because its color looked like the stone from the Isle of Portland.
strings.12-03.name: Reinforced concrete
strings.12-03.hee1: Reinforced concrete was born from flower pots.
strings.12-04.name: Steel frame construction
strings.12-04.hee1: The height of the Eiffel Tower changes by more than ten centimeters between summer and winter.
strings.12-05.name: Flat glass
strings.12-05.hee1: Window glass is made by "floating it on melted metal".
strings.12-06.name: Water supply
strings.12-06.hee1: Tiny living things in a layer of sand clean the water.
strings.12-07.name: Chlorination
strings.12-07.hee1: The smell of a swimming pool is the smell of the chlorine that keeps away disease.
strings.12-08.name: Sewer system
strings.12-08.hee1: It started because the smell got so bad that Parliament could not meet.
strings.12-09.name: Roads
strings.12-09.hee1: "Tarmac" comes from coal tar and Mr. McAdam's name.
strings.12-10.name: Bridge
strings.12-10.hee1: A frame of triangles (a truss) does not lose its shape.
strings.12-11.name: Surveying
strings.12-11.hee1: Tadataka Ino measured all of Japan with his footsteps.
strings.12-12.name: Ventilation and air conditioning
strings.12-12.hee1: Air conditioning was born not for people, but for paper.
strings.12-13.name: HEPA filter
strings.12-13.hee1: The hardest size of particle to catch is 0.3 µm.
strings.12-14.name: Laminar-flow cleanroom
strings.12-14.hee1: Chips are made in rooms thousands of times cleaner than an operating room.
strings.12-15.name: Lightning rod
strings.12-15.hee1: The lightning rod in Minecraft is made of copper, just like the real one.
strings.12-16.name: Elevator safety brake
strings.12-16.hee1: Otis did not invent the elevator; what he made was a catch so that it "does not fall even if the rope breaks".
strings.12-17.name: Electric elevator and counterweight
strings.12-17.hee1: On the other end of an elevator's rope hangs a weight about as heavy as the car, so the motor only lifts the "difference in weight".
strings.12-18.name: Rock drill
strings.12-18.hee1: Rock drills driven by air even made the air inside the tunnel easier to breathe, using the air they had finished with.
strings.13-01.name: Soap and handwashing
strings.13-01.hee1: The doctor who told people to wash their hands was laughed at for as long as he lived.
strings.13-02.name: Antisepsis
strings.13-02.hee1: The mouthwash Listerine is named after Lister.
strings.13-03.name: Anesthesia
strings.13-03.hee1: The world's first operation under general anesthesia was done in Japan.
strings.13-04.name: Bacteriology
strings.13-04.hee1: Diseases were passed on by living things too small to see.
strings.13-05.name: Agar medium
strings.13-05.hee1: Research on bacteria moved forward thanks to a kitchen trick from jam-making.
strings.13-06.name: Vaccine
strings.13-06.hee1: The word vaccine comes from the Latin word for "cow".
strings.13-07.name: Epidemiology
strings.13-07.hee1: Just putting dots on a map found the cause of a disease.
strings.13-08.name: Aspirin
strings.13-08.hee1: How the medicine works was found out more than 70 years after it went on sale.
strings.13-09.name: Sulfa drugs
strings.13-09.hee1: The first germ-killing drug was a dye for coloring cloth.
strings.13-10.name: Penicillin
strings.13-10.hee1: The mold used for mass production was found on a rotten melon from a market.
strings.13-11.name: X-ray diagnosis
strings.13-11.hee1: Röntgen did not take out a patent, so that anyone could use it.
strings.13-12.name: Blood transfusion and blood types
strings.13-12.hee1: Until blood types were known, a transfusion was a gamble.
strings.13-13.name: Thermometer
strings.13-13.hee1: Old thermometers were as long as 30 cm.
strings.13-14.name: Fluoride and teeth
strings.13-14.hee1: The fluorine in toothpaste is the same element as the fluorine in excimer lasers.
strings.13-15.name: Medical oxygen
strings.13-15.hee1: Hospital oxygen is taken out of air that has been turned into liquid.
strings.13-16.name: Tying off blood vessels to stop bleeding
strings.13-16.hee1: A surgeon who started out as a barber found a gentler treatment, thanks to running out of oil.
strings.14-01.name: Canals and locks
strings.14-01.hee1: On a canal's staircase, ships climb mountains.
strings.14-02.name: Compass
strings.14-02.hee1: A compass needle moves because the Earth itself is a giant magnet.
strings.14-03.name: Longitude and the chronometer
strings.14-03.hee1: How accurate a clock was decided where a ship was.
strings.14-04.name: Steamship
strings.14-04.hee1: Ships that could move without wind made the world smaller.
strings.14-05.name: Railways
strings.14-05.hee1: The width between the rails is said to come from the width of horse-cart wheels ⚠️
strings.14-06.name: Steel rails
strings.14-06.hee1: Steel rails lasted more than 10 times as long as iron rails ⚠️
strings.14-07.name: Pneumatic tire
strings.14-07.hee1: The air-filled tire was made by an animal doctor for his child.
strings.14-08.name: Bicycle
strings.14-08.hee1: The first bicycles had no pedals.
strings.14-09.name: Internal combustion engine
strings.14-09.hee1: An engine's four beats are "suck, squeeze, burn, blow out".
strings.14-10.name: Diesel engine
strings.14-10.hee1: A diesel engine ran on peanut oil.
strings.14-11.name: Automobile
strings.14-11.hee1: The first long-distance drive was a wife's trip with her children, kept secret from her husband.
strings.14-12.name: Airplane
strings.14-12.hee1: The Wright brothers ran a bicycle shop.
strings.14-13.name: Duralumin
strings.14-13.hee1: Left alone over a weekend, the metal had gone hard all by itself.
strings.14-14.name: Electric railway
strings.14-14.hee1: Subways were only possible with electricity, which makes no smoke.
strings.14-15.name: Rocket equation
strings.14-15.hee1: Even in space, where there is no air to push against, a rocket moves by the kick of its own exhaust.
strings.14-16.name: Self-driving cars
strings.14-16.hee1: In the first driverless car race, not one car finished; even the car that got farthest covered only about one twentieth of the course.
strings.14-17.name: Air brake
strings.14-17.hee1: The air brake is built to "stop when the air leaks out", so even when it breaks, it fails on the safe side.
strings.14-18.name: Drum brakes and disc brakes
strings.14-18.hee1: Brakes stop a car by turning its motion into "heat", so they can get too hot going down a mountain road.
strings.14-19.name: Automatic transmission
strings.14-19.hee1: The first mass-produced automatic transmission changed gears by "oil pressure", not by pressing pedals.
strings.14-20.name: Turbocharger
strings.14-20.hee1: A turbo uses the push of the exhaust gas, which would have been thrown away, to force air into the engine.
strings.14-21.name: E6B flight computer
strings.14-21.hee1: A calculator you spin round and round, with no battery. Pilots still use it in training today.
strings.14-22.name: Assembly line and conveyor belt
strings.14-22.hee1: The assembly line made cars cheap, so even the workers could buy a Model T.
strings.14-23.name: Overhead transport (OHT)
strings.14-23.hee1: On the ceiling of a semiconductor factory, kilometers of rails and hundreds of little carts are running.
strings.15-01.name: Paper
strings.15-01.hee1: Paper used to be made from rags; today it is made from wood.
strings.15-02.name: Movable-type printing
strings.15-02.hee1: Type metal is a rare alloy that swells as it sets.
strings.15-03.name: Submarine cable
strings.15-03.hee1: The cable's insulation was rubber made from tree sap.
strings.15-04.name: Telephone
strings.15-04.hee1: Telephone microphones were made of grains of carbon.
strings.15-05.name: Phonograph
strings.15-05.hee1: The first words ever recorded were "Mary Had a Little Lamb".
strings.15-06.name: Discovery of radio waves
strings.15-06.hee1: Hertz said, "This discovery is of no use at all" ⚠️
strings.15-07.name: Wireless telegraphy
strings.15-07.hee1: When the Titanic sank, some people were saved in time thanks to radio.
strings.15-08.name: Crystal radio
strings.15-08.hee1: The point-contact transistor's "needle standing on a crystal" is a descendant of the crystal radio.
strings.15-09.name: Vacuum tube radio
strings.15-09.hee1: At first, radios were as big as furniture.
strings.15-10.name: Transistor radio
strings.15-10.hee1: In 1954, a radio using transistors went on sale.
strings.15-11.name: Television
strings.15-11.hee1: The first picture on Japanese television was the katakana letter "イ" (i).
strings.15-12.name: Magnetic recording
strings.15-12.hee1: The brown on a cassette tape is rusted iron powder.
strings.15-13.name: Optical fiber
strings.15-13.hee1: Cables of light running along the sea floor carry the world's internet.
strings.15-14.name: Information theory
strings.15-14.hee1: The word "bit" spread through Shannon's paper.
strings.15-15.name: Computer networks
strings.15-15.hee1: The first message over a network stopped after two letters, "LO" (it crashed partway through LOGIN).
strings.15-16.name: USB
strings.15-16.hee1: Before USB, computers had several differently shaped sockets: one for the mouse, one for the keyboard, one for the printer.
strings.15-17.name: Wi-Fi
strings.15-17.hee1: "Wi-Fi" is not short for anything; it is a name chosen to be easy to remember.
strings.15-18.name: Capacitive touchscreen
strings.15-18.hee1: Just bringing your finger close is enough for the invisible electrodes under the screen to notice "there is a finger here".
strings.15-19.name: Loudspeaker
strings.15-19.hee1: A loudspeaker makes sound by shaking paper with a magnet and a coil of wire (a cousin of the motor).
strings.15-20.name: Mobile phone radio
strings.15-20.hee1: The world's first mobile phone network was the car phone in Tokyo in 1979.
strings.15-21.name: Bluetooth
strings.15-21.hee1: Bluetooth is named after "Bluetooth", the nickname of an old king who united countries.
strings.15-22.name: Antenna
strings.15-22.hee1: The length of an antenna is set by the wavelength of the radio waves it picks up. For a smartphone's Wi-Fi, it is about 3 cm.
strings.15-23.name: Condenser microphone
strings.15-23.hee1: Recording-studio microphones catch sound with the gap between a very thin film that moves with the sound and a plate.
strings.15-24.name: Dynamic microphone
strings.15-24.hee1: A karaoke microphone works the same way as a speaker used backwards.
strings.15-25.name: Electret condenser microphone
strings.15-25.hee1: Many of the microphones in phones and toys are made of a plastic film that keeps an electric charge stored inside it.
strings.15-26.name: MEMS microphone
strings.15-26.hee1: A smartphone has several tiny microphones carved out of silicon, and they are also used to cancel noise.
strings.15-27.name: Yagi-Uda antenna
strings.15-27.hee1: The rods lined up on a rooftop TV antenna are shaped to gather radio waves from one direction.
strings.15-28.name: Optical disc
strings.15-28.hee1: A scratched CD still plays because the broken parts are fixed by calculation.
strings.15-29.name: Error-correcting code
strings.15-29.hee1: QR codes have extra information hidden inside so they can still be read when a little dirty or chipped.
strings.15-30.name: Public-key cryptography
strings.15-30.hee1: You can shop online because of the math of a "lock" that anyone can close but only you can open.
strings.15-31.name: Rotary-head videotape
strings.15-31.hee1: Videotape had a small head spinning faster than the tape, writing the picture on a slant.
strings.15-32.name: Semaphore telegraph
strings.15-32.hee1: News that took a day by horse could reach Paris in under an hour by a relay of towers.
strings.15-33.name: Hellschreiber
strings.15-33.hee1: Letters were sent as pictures, so even if noise wiped out some dots, a person could still read them.
strings.B-01.name: Incandescent light bulb
strings.B-01.hee1: The vacuum tube was born from adding one plate inside a light bulb.
strings.B-02.name: Silver halide photography
strings.B-02.hee1: The ancestor of photolithography (setting up Chapter 3, [7-11]).
strings.B-02a.name: Daguerreotype
strings.B-02a.hee1: Each picture is one of a kind and cannot be copied (there is no negative).
strings.B-02b.name: Wet plate photography → gelatin dry plate
strings.B-02b.hee1: Many prints from one glass negative = the photolithography idea of copying many times from one mask.
strings.B-03.name: X-ray tube
strings.B-03.hee1: X-rays were named X because they were "rays of unknown nature".
strings.B-04.name: Magnetron and microwave oven
strings.B-04.hee1: The microwave oven was born from a radar part.
strings.B-05.name: Polarization
strings.B-05.hee1: Put a clear calcite crystal on some writing, and the letters look doubled.
strings.B-06.name: Polarizing film
strings.B-06.hee1: In front of an LCD screen is a film dyed with iodine.
strings.B-07.name: LED
strings.B-07.hee1: Only after the blue LED was made could white LEDs finally be made.
strings.B-08.name: Electronic calculator
strings.B-08.hee1: The first calculator weighed as much as a desk.
strings.B-09.name: Game console
strings.B-09.hee1: The Famicom's CPU is a grandchild of the technology that gave birth to the calculator.
strings.B-10.name: Smartphone
strings.B-10.hee1: In your pocket, millions of times the computing power of the Apollo computer.
strings.B-11.name: AI chip
strings.B-11.hee1: Starting from stone tools, you reach the parts of a thinking machine.
strings.B-12.name: Solar cell
strings.B-12.hee1: A solar cell uses the same p-n junction as a transistor.
strings.B-13.name: Mauveine
strings.B-13.hee1: The chemical industry began from a failed experiment to make a medicine.
strings.B-14.name: Acetylene lamp
strings.B-14.hee1: A stone that gives off a gas that burns when you drip water on it.
strings.B-15.name: Tofu
strings.B-15.hee1: From nigari, which sets tofu, you can get magnesium metal ([1-39]).
strings.B-16.name: Personal computer
strings.B-16.hee1: Computers that sit on a desk all went on sale at once in 1977.
strings.B-17.name: GPS
strings.B-17.hee1: From the tiny time differences of signals coming from satellites in the sky, you can tell where you are.
strings.B-18.name: Liquid crystal display
strings.B-18.hee1: Liquid crystal does not glow by itself; electricity turns it to open and close the path for light.
strings.B-19.name: TFT LCD
strings.B-19.hee1: Behind each pixel of the screen is one thin transistor, and millions of them are lined up on glass.
strings.B-20.name: White LED backlight
strings.B-20.hee1: Inside a white LED is a blue LED covered with a powder that glows yellow; blue and yellow mix to look white.
strings.B-21.name: Ball mouse
strings.B-21.hee1: The first mouse was a wooden box with two wheels, not a ball.
strings.B-22.name: Optical mouse
strings.B-22.hee1: An optical mouse takes more than 1000 pictures of the desk surface every second and works out its movement from how the pattern shifts.
strings.B-23.name: Dissolved acetylene and the automatic lighthouse flasher
strings.B-23.hee1: Old lighthouses had a device inside that sensed daylight and put the flame out by itself during the day.
strings.B-24.name: Nixie tube
strings.B-24.hee1: Ten pieces of metal shaped like the digits sit inside, one on top of another.
strings.P-01.name: Crane
strings.P-01.hee1: The stones of Greek temples still have holes and grooves for cranes to grip them.
strings.P-02.name: Liquid-fuel rocket
strings.P-02.hee1: The first liquid-fuel rocket flew for only about 2.5 seconds.
strings.P-03.name: Electric car
strings.P-03.hee1: Cars that run on electricity were already on the road in 1881, before gasoline cars.
strings.P-04.name: 3D printer (light-curing type)
strings.P-04.hee1: The first paper on 3D printing was written by a Japanese researcher.
strings.P-05.name: 3D printer (melted-plastic layering type)
strings.P-05.hee1: The 3D printer was born from making a toy with a glue gun.
strings.P-06.name: Your computer
strings.P-06.hee1: The computer in front of you holds inventions from many different times, from the typewriter of 150 years ago to the GPU of 1999.
strings.P-07.name: Monitor
strings.P-07.hee1: The colors on a screen are made only from mixing the brightness of red, green and blue dots.
strings.P-08.name: Mouse
strings.P-08.hee1: The first mouse was a wooden box with two wheels.
strings.P-09.name: Computer keyboard
strings.P-09.hee1: The keys are still in the same order as on typewriters 150 years ago.
strings.P-10.name: Cooling
strings.P-10.hee1: Without cooling, a computer's chip would reach a dangerous temperature in a few seconds.
strings.P-11.name: Power supply unit
strings.P-11.hee1: The power supply box is small because it switches the electricity on and off tens of thousands of times a second.
strings.P-12.name: CPU
strings.P-12.hee1: Today's CPUs have millions of times as many transistors as the 4004.
strings.P-13.name: Computer GPU
strings.P-13.hee1: The shadows and light on Minecraft blocks are worked out all at the same time by thousands of calculators in the GPU.
strings.P-14.name: Memory
strings.P-14.hee1: Memory rewrites itself dozens of times a second so that it does not forget.
strings.P-15.name: Computer SSD
strings.P-15.hee1: Your Minecraft world save is remembered by electrons shut inside the SSD.
strings.P-16.name: Smartphone screen
strings.P-16.hee1: A smartphone screen is a sandwich of many layers: glass, invisible electrodes, and the display.
strings.P-17.name: Smartphone camera
strings.P-17.hee1: A smartphone camera and the eye of an optical mouse are the same family of chip.
strings.P-18.name: Motion sensor
strings.P-18.hee1: The screen turns when you tip your smartphone sideways because a tiny weight inside moves.
strings.P-19.name: Smartphone vibration motor
strings.P-19.hee1: The buzz of silent mode is a lopsided weight spinning inside.
strings.P-20.name: Smartphone speaker
strings.P-20.hee1: Even the tiny speaker in a smartphone has a strong neodymium magnet inside.
strings.P-21.name: Radio chips and antennas
strings.P-21.hee1: A smartphone's GPS only "listens" to radio waves; it sends nothing to the satellites.
strings.P-22.name: Battery
strings.P-22.hee1: In a smartphone battery, lithium moves in and out of the gaps in graphite.
strings.P-23.name: Memory chip
strings.P-23.hee1: The photos on your phone are remembered by the number of electrons shut inside a chip.
strings.P-24.name: Humanoid robot
strings.P-24.hee1: The humanoid robot built at Waseda University in 1973 could not only walk but also speak simple Japanese.
strings.P-25.name: Robot arm
strings.P-25.hee1: The first factory robot arm was moved not by electric motors but by oil pressure.
strings.P-26.name: Self-driving car
strings.P-26.hee1: The car that won the 2005 driverless car race finished the desert course in about 7 hours with no one on board.
strings.P-27.name: Digital camera
strings.P-27.hee1: The first test digital camera (1975) recorded its pictures on a cassette tape.
strings.P-28.name: Microphone
strings.P-28.hee1: A karaoke microphone works the same way as a speaker used backwards.
strings.P-29.name: Air conditioner
strings.P-29.hee1: An air conditioner does not make cold; it carries the room's heat outside.
strings.P-30.name: Refrigerator
strings.P-30.hee1: A refrigerator throws the heat from inside out into the room from its back and sides (that is why the back of a fridge is warm).
strings.P-31.name: Coffee machine
strings.P-31.hee1: Espresso is made by pushing hot water through coffee grounds at about 9 atmospheres, about 4 times the pressure in a tire.
strings.P-32.name: Robot vacuum
